subject: system
statement: The Download ADMX dialog lets any typed or browsed folder be the destination. When run as administrator it takes ownership, grants Administrators full control and resets permissions, and for any user it deletes and replaces same-named files there. Nothing checks the folder is a policy-definitions folder.

subject: system
statement: The ADMX download trusts a Microsoft installer package on HTTPS alone: no hash or signature check, older TLS allowed, then unpacked and its files replace same-named files in the policy folder. A tampered package would place attacker-chosen definitions there. Reach is this download only.

subject: system
statement: The installer program is launched by bare name, so the system search order decides which executable runs. Scratch and unpack folders are fixed names, not emptied before use, so leftovers of a failed run can reach the next unpack.

subject: system
statement: As administrator, the program can load another user's registry file into the machine registry, from a profile folder list or a path the user chooses. It is administrator-only and rests on user-chosen paths, with no further check.

subject: system
statement: A typed user identifier for a policy source is joined into a file path under the system folder and written to, without checking its form. A crafted value could point the write elsewhere.

subject: system
statement: Every web request, including the installer download, permits the deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 beside 1.2, to keep Windows Vista working. A weaker protocol could be negotiated; the code does not show an older version actually being used.

subject: system
statement: The program is built for .NET Framework 4.5.2, whose Microsoft support has ended. Findings differ on weight: newer Windows runs it on a still-supported 4.x runtime, so the exposure is the old build target, not the runtime in use.

subject: system
statement: The policy-version file is rewritten in place after being read. A failure midway leaves it truncated, so Windows may not notice a policy change.

subject: system
statement: A package fetched over HTTPS from one fixed Microsoft address is unpacked with no signature or hash check by this code. A substituted package, or a compromised trust store or proxy, would put altered definitions into the destination, by default the Windows policy folder.

subject: system
statement: Saving can fail without the person knowing. Unwritable sources are skipped yet the message says success, a failed comment save is ignored, and settings that cannot be stored silently do not persist. An edit or choice may be believed kept when it was not.

subject: system
statement: Results of enabling privileges and loading a registry file are ignored. If either fails the program carries on without saying why, and a later save can fail or be silently skipped.

subject: system
statement: The ADMX download and unpack have no timeout or cancel, and the dialog refuses to close while they run. A stalled connection or hung installer leaves the dialog and its owner window unusable until the process is killed.

subject: system
statement: The ADMX download deletes each same-named file before moving its replacement, not atomically. A failure part-way can leave the destination, by default the system policy folder, with mixed old and new files and changed ownership. Errors show only a generic message and the scratch folder is left behind.

subject: system
statement: The download address and the folder inside the package are pinned to one release, Windows 11 26H2, on Microsoft's download site. If Microsoft moves the file or renames the folder, the download fails until the code is edited; later releases are not picked up.
